name: Grammar Quest
tagline: Articles, tenses, conditionals and confusing words.
label: FILL IN THE GAP

levels.title: A, an, the or nothing?
levels.question: Use “a” before a consonant sound and “an” before a vowel sound.
rule: Use “a” before a consonant sound and “an” before a vowel sound.
Use “the” for something identifiable; sometimes no article is needed.

items.why: Umbrella begins with a vowel sound.
Elephant begins with a vowel sound.
Honest begins with a vowel sound.

items.text: I met ___ teacher who helped me yesterday.
items.why: The relative clause identifies the teacher.
Hour begins with a vowel sound.

levels.title: Much, many, little and few
levels.question: Use “many/few” with countable plurals and “much/little” with uncountable nouns.
rule: Use “many/few” with countable plurals and “much/little” with uncountable nouns.
“A few” and “a little” mean some.

items.why: A few pupils means some pupils.

items.text: There is ___ sugar in the jar.

items.why: Chairs are countable; more works for both types.

items.text: There are ___ buses today than yesterday.
The pot contains ___ soup than before.

levels.title: Past or present perfect?
levels.question: Use the simple past for a finished time such as yesterday.
rule: Use the simple past for a finished time such as yesterday.
Use the present perfect for past actions connected to now; do not pair it with a finished-time expression.

items.text: He ___ his bag two hours ago.

items.why: Just marks a recent event connected to now.
Monday is a specified finished time here.

items.text: They ___ worked here for five years and still do.
She ___ finished her homework before dinner yesterday.
items.why: Past perfect marks an earlier past event.

levels.title: Conditionals
levels.question: Use present + present for general truths; present + will for real future possibilities; past + would for imagined situations; had + would have for imagined past outcomes.
rule: Use present + present for general truths; present + will for real future possibilities; past + would for imagined situations; had + would have for imagined past outcomes.

items.text: If water freezes, it ___ into ice.
items.why: Zero conditional describes a general truth.

items.text: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ indoors.
If I had wings, I ___ fly.
If he had left earlier, he ___ have caught the bus.
If I were the captain, I ___ change the plan.
If they arrive early, we ___ start at once.
If I had known, I ___ have called.
If you press this button, the light ___.

levels.title: Commonly confused words
levels.question: Choose by meaning and grammatical function.
rule: Choose by meaning and grammatical function.
Similar spelling does not make words interchangeable.

items.why: Principal means head of a school.

items.text: Please ___ me on the next step.

name: Meaning Match
tagline: Find the word closest in meaning.
label: CLOSEST IN MEANING

levels.title: Everyday meaning
levels.question: Choose the closest meaning in the sentence, not just a vaguely related word.
rule: Choose the closest meaning in the sentence, not just a vaguely related word.

items.text: He was DELIGHTED by the news.
They live in a REMOTE village.

levels.title: Feelings and character
levels.question: Pay attention to the strength of each word and the situation in which it is used.
rule: Pay attention to the strength of each word and the situation in which it is used.

items.text: Bola was ANXIOUS before the exam.

levels.title: Academic vocabulary
levels.question: Use the sentence to work out the intended meaning of more formal words.
rule: Use the sentence to work out the intended meaning of more formal words.

items.why: Feasible means possible to carry out.

levels.title: Meaning in context
levels.question: A word can have several meanings.
rule: A word can have several meanings.
Choose the one that fits the particular sentence.

items.text: The principal gave a SOUND argument.
The judge took a FIRM position.
The speaker made a POINTED remark.
The shop is CLOSE to the school.

items.why: Struck means came suddenly to mind.

levels.title: Everyday opposites
levels.question: Choose the word that is most opposite in meaning in the sentence.
rule: Choose the word that is most opposite in meaning in the sentence.

items.why: Closed is the opposite of open.

levels.title: Character and feelings
levels.question: Find the most natural opposite for the meaning used in the sentence.
rule: Find the most natural opposite for the meaning used in the sentence.

items.why: Impatient is the opposite of patient.

levels.title: Formal vocabulary
levels.question: Pay attention to prefixes, but do not assume every prefix gives the right opposite.
rule: Pay attention to prefixes, but do not assume every prefix gives the right opposite.

levels.title: Opposites in context
levels.question: Choose the opposite of the highlighted meaning, not another meaning of the same word.
rule: Choose the opposite of the highlighted meaning, not another meaning of the same word.

levels.title: Short /ɪ/ and long /iː/
levels.question: Compare ship /ʃɪp/ and sheep /ʃiːp/.
rule: Compare ship /ʃɪp/ and sheep /ʃiːp/.
Spellings can mislead: listen to the vowel in the dictionary pronunciation.

items.text: Which has the vowel /iː/: ship or sheep?
Which rhymes with meet: fit or feet?
Which rhymes with bit: beat or sit?

items.why: women /ˈwɪmɪn/ has /ɪ/ in its first syllable.

items.text: Which rhymes with sheep: cheap or chip?

levels.title: Short /ʊ/ and long /uː/
levels.question: Compare full /fʊl/ and fool /fuːl/.
rule: Compare full /fʊl/ and fool /fuːl/.
The spelling “oo” does not always signal /uː/.

items.text: Which rhymes with book: look or Luke?
Which rhymes with fool: cool or full?

levels.title: Consonant contrasts
levels.question: Compare think /θɪŋk/ with this /ðɪs/, and sip /sɪp/ with zip /zɪp/.
rule: Compare think /θɪŋk/ with this /ðɪs/, and sip /sɪp/ with zip /zɪp/.

items.text: Which begins with /θ/: think or this?
Which begins with /ð/: then or thin?
Which begins with /s/: sip or zip?
Which begins with /z/: zoo or sue?
Which begins with /ʃ/: ship or chip?
Which begins with /tʃ/: chair or share?
Which begins with /dʒ/: jam or yam?
Which begins with /ʃ/: shoe or chew?
Which begins with /θ/: three or tree?
Which begins with /ð/: those or toes?

levels.title: Silent letters
levels.question: Some written letters are not pronounced.
rule: Some written letters are not pronounced.
Learn the spoken form, not the spelling alone.

items.text: Which letter is silent in knife?
Which letter is silent in write?
Which letter is silent in honest?
Which letter is silent in debt?
Which letter is silent in lamb?
Which letter is silent in castle?
Which letter is silent in doubt?
Which letter is silent in island?
Which letter is silent in comb?
Which letter is silent in knee?

levels.title: First or second syllable?
levels.question: One syllable is stronger.
rule: One syllable is stronger.
TAble stresses the first; beGIN stresses the second.
Capitals show the strong syllable.

items.text: Which syllable is stressed in table?
Which syllable is stressed in begin?
Which syllable is stressed in happy?
Which syllable is stressed in relax?
Which syllable is stressed in window?
Which syllable is stressed in decide?
Which syllable is stressed in teacher?
Which syllable is stressed in enjoy?
Which syllable is stressed in garden?
Which syllable is stressed in arrive?

levels.title: Noun and verb pairs
levels.question: Some two-syllable words change stress with their job: a REcord (noun), to reCORD (verb).
rule: Some two-syllable words change stress with their job: a REcord (noun), to reCORD (verb).

items.why: PROtest is a noun in standard British pronunciation.
proTEST is the verb in standard British pronunciation.

levels.title: Three-syllable words
levels.question: Do not assume all three-syllable words stress the same position.
rule: Do not assume all three-syllable words stress the same position.
Learn common word families.

levels.title: Stress and suffixes
levels.question: In words ending -tion, -ic and -ity, stress often comes before the ending.
rule: In words ending -tion, -ic and -ity, stress often comes before the ending.
Learn the whole word and verify exceptions.

name: Idiom Decoder
tagline: Crack idioms, phrasal verbs and proverbs.
label: WHAT DOES IT MEAN?

levels.title: Common everyday idioms
levels.question: Idioms have meanings beyond their literal words.
rule: Idioms have meanings beyond their literal words.
Use the sentence to choose the intended meaning.

items.text: Chidi threw in the towel after many attempts.
items.why: Throw in the towel means stop trying.

items.text: The maths test was a piece of cake for Bola.
items.why: A piece of cake means easy.

items.text: Hauwa broke the ice with a joke.
items.why: Break the ice means ease tension.

items.text: The secret is out of the bag.
items.why: Out of the bag means no longer secret.

items.text: Emeka is on cloud nine after the result.
Ade hit the nail on the head.
items.why: Hit the nail on the head means be exactly right.

items.text: Ngozi kept an eye on the bag.
items.why: Keep an eye on means watch.

items.text: The new phone cost an arm and a leg.
items.why: Costs an arm and a leg means costly.

items.text: The coach told them to pull their socks up.
items.why: Pull your socks up means improve effort.

levels.title: Phrasal verbs
levels.question: A verb plus a small word can create a new meaning.
rule: A verb plus a small word can create a new meaning.
Learn it in a full sentence.

items.text: Please look up the word in a dictionary.
The meeting was put off until Friday.
The bus broke down on the way.
He ran into an old friend.
items.why: Run into means encounter by chance.

items.text: The teacher called off the trip.
She came across an old photograph.

levels.title: Expressions in context
levels.question: Similar-looking expressions can mean different things.
rule: Similar-looking expressions can mean different things.
Read the full sentence.

items.text: The new pupil felt like a fish out of water.
items.why: Fish out of water means out of place.

items.text: Bola decided to turn over a new leaf.
items.why: Turn over a new leaf means improve behaviour.

items.text: The news came out of the blue.
items.why: Out of the blue means without warning.

items.text: The team went the extra mile.
items.why: Go the extra mile means do more than required.

items.text: The teacher gave us the green light.
The instructions went over his head.
items.why: Go over someone’s head means be beyond understanding.

items.text: The friends agreed to bury the hatchet.
items.why: Bury the hatchet means make peace.

items.text: The plan is still up in the air.
items.why: Up in the air means unsettled.

items.text: She learned the speech by heart.

levels.title: Proverbs and sayings
levels.question: A proverb communicates a general lesson.
rule: A proverb communicates a general lesson.
Interpret its message, not just its literal image.

items.text: A stitch in time saves nine.
items.answer: Act early to prevent bigger problems
options: Act early to prevent bigger problems
Too many people directing a task can ruin it
Attractive things may lack real value
Act early to prevent bigger problems
Do not assume success too early
Too many people directing a task can ruin it
Act early to prevent bigger problems

items.answer: Too many people directing a task can ruin it

options: What people do matters more than promises

items.text: Where there is a will, there is a way.
options: Do not assume success too early

items.text: Do not count your chickens before they hatch.
items.answer: Do not assume success too early
options: Do not assume success too early
What people do matters more than promises
items.why: Wait for a result before relying on it.

items.text: The early bird catches the worm.
options: Attractive things may lack real value

name: Context Clues
tagline: Work out meaning from the words around it.
label: READ THE CLUES

levels.title: Meaning from nearby words
levels.question: Read what happens before and after the unfamiliar word.
rule: Read what happens before and after the unfamiliar word.
The surrounding sentence often explains it.

items.text: After walking all day, the hikers were famished and ate immediately. What is famished?
items.why: They ate immediately after a long walk.

items.text: The fragile glass broke when it fell. What is fragile?
Despite the noise, Hauwa remained focused on her book. What is focused?
items.why: She continued attending to her book.

items.text: The road was slippery after the rain. What is slippery?
items.why: Rain makes the road hard to grip.

items.text: The child was reluctant and needed encouragement to join. What is reluctant?
The shop was deserted; nobody was inside. What is deserted?
The explanation was concise: only two sentences. What is concise?
He was punctual and arrived at exactly eight. What is punctual?
items.why: The arrival matched the scheduled time.

items.text: The twins look alike, but their personalities differ. What does differ mean?
The queue was enormous and stretched outside the building. What is enormous?

levels.title: Contrast clues
levels.question: Words such as but, although, whereas and unlike can reveal an opposite meaning.
rule: Words such as but, although, whereas and unlike can reveal an opposite meaning.

items.text: Unlike his timid brother, Tunde spoke confidently. Timid means?
The first test was easy, but the second was arduous. Arduous means?
Although the road was narrow, the highway was broad. Broad means?
The room was usually noisy; today it was tranquil. Tranquil means?
Her old phone was unreliable, whereas the new one was dependable. Dependable means?
Bola is generous, but her cousin is miserly. Miserly means?
The instructions seemed vague, but the diagram was explicit. Explicit means?
The first offer was rejected; the second was accepted. Rejected means?
Although the journey was brief, the wait was prolonged. Prolonged means?
The bag was lightweight, unlike the bulky suitcase. Bulky means?
items.why: Unlike signals a contrast in handling.

levels.title: Inference from actions
levels.question: Infer only what the text supports.
rule: Infer only what the text supports.
Do not add details that are not stated.

items.text: Ade checked his watch three times and hurried towards the gate. What is likely?
options: She wanted to understand the task
items.why: Checking time and hurrying suggest urgency.

items.text: Ngozi reread the instructions before answering. What can we infer?
items.answer: She wanted to understand the task
options: She wanted to understand the task

items.text: The crowd stood and applauded after the performance. How did they respond?
options: She wanted to understand the task

items.text: Emeka returned the extra change to the cashier. What trait is shown?
options: The room was not in use at that moment
items.why: He returned money that was not his.

items.text: Hauwa carried an umbrella after seeing dark clouds. Why?
The classroom lights were off and the door was locked. What is most likely?
items.answer: The room was not in use at that moment
options: The room was not in use at that moment
items.why: Locked door and lights off support this.

items.text: The player trained daily before the competition. What is suggested?
The pupils whispered while the baby slept. Why?
options: The room was not in use at that moment
She wanted to understand the task

items.text: Bola saved part of her allowance every week. What does this show?
The shopkeeper lowered prices after customers complained. What prompted the change?

levels.title: Tone and purpose
levels.question: Tone is the writer’s attitude; purpose is what the writer wants to achieve.
rule: Tone is the writer’s attitude; purpose is what the writer wants to achieve.
Look for clues in word choice.

items.text: “Please submit your forms by Friday.” Main purpose?
items.why: It gives an action and deadline.

items.text: “The bridge was completed in 2019.” Main purpose?
“You should wear a helmet when cycling.” Main purpose?
“Try our new service today!” Main purpose?
“Do not touch the wet paint.” Main purpose?
“The library opens at nine.” Main purpose?
“Thank you for your thoughtful help.” Tone?
